extracted.intended_audience: researchers in health psychology and positive psychology (meta-analysts and empirical investigators)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical synthesis for evaluating the effect of subjective well-being on objective health outcomes, including moderators (study design, outcome type, operationalization, sample characteristics) and recommended measurement/analysis practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect size interpretation (r → BESD → OR/RR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effect sizes (Pearson r) should be interpreted practically using a binomial effect size display (BESD). The BESD is most easily understood when the outcome is dichotomous (e.g., survival).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convert aggregate r to a BESD to express differences in probabilities (example: r = 0.14 → 14% higher probability of living longer for high vs low well-being). BESD can then be translated into relative risk (RR) and odds ratio (OR) (example: OR ≈ 1.75; RR ≈ 0.75). See Rosenthal (1991, 1994) and Rosenthal & DiMatteo (2001) for conversion steps and rationale. Use these translations when balancing costs/benefits of interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study design as moderator (experimental vs longitudinal vs ambulatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Study design materially moderates observed effects: experimental studies show the strongest effects; longitudinal and ambulatory studies typically show smaller effects, with ambulatory often near zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer experimental designs to infer causal impact because of greater control over extraneous variables. Ambulatory studies may measure transient emotions that are influenced by many external factors (weather, time of day, daily hassles), producing attenuated associations. When synthesizing, analyze designs separately and consider reasons (measurement, extraneous psychosocial factors) for differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health outcome typology (short-term vs long-term vs disease/symptom control)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate health outcomes as short-term states, long-term processes, or disease/symptom control; well-being impacts vary by outcome type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect stronger effects of well-being on short-term outcomes (e.g., immune functioning, pain tolerance) because fewer intervening variables operate. Long-term outcomes (e.g., cardiovascular events, survival) are influenced by multiple complex factors over time, so trait-level well-being may be more relevant. Analyze outcome types separately in meta-analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalization of well-being (state vs trait)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether well-being is measured/manipulated as a transient state or as a trait affects which health outcomes it relates to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State manipulations of well-being are more strongly associated with short-term health outcomes (infections, immune response); trait measures are more strongly associated with long-term outcomes (cardiovascular outcomes, survival). Choose operationalization to match the target health outcome when designing studies or interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific physiological marker sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Different physiological markers show heterogeneous associations with positive affect and well-being (e.g., sIgA strongly related; cortisol shows significant drops; other stress hormones non-significant; blood pressure marginal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider measurement ease and biological plausibility: sIgA (saliva) may show stronger effects partly because it is easy to measure. Cortisol is particularly susceptible to emotional triggers. When selecting biomarkers, report which markers were used and interpret differential sensitivity across markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambulatory methodology limitations and recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambulatory studies produced significantly lower effect sizes and often non-significant results across many health outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate whether ambulatory studies focused on a narrow set of outcomes; improve well-being measures for ambulatory contexts; develop appropriate statistical techniques (e.g., multilevel modeling) and determine how to conceptualize and measure health outcomes across lab and field settings. Recognize that fewer ambulatory studies exist and methods are still being refined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample-specific moderators (initial health status, age, gender composition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sample characteristics moderate well-being–health relations: initial health status, age, and gender composition influence effect sizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report and analyze sample characteristics. Examples: well-being had greater impact on short- and long-term outcomes in healthy samples but more effect on disease control and survival in unhealthy samples; age moderated cardiovascular/physiological reactivity (older individuals benefited via decreased reactivity); male-dominated samples showed decreased strength for some immune effects and stronger long-term functioning effects for males. Use sample composition in meta-regressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting completeness (demographics like ethnicity and marital status)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many primary studies did not report participant ethnicity or marital status, preventing moderator analyses on these variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage primary researchers to report descriptive statistics (ethnicity, marital status, etc.) routinely so future meta-analyses can test for moderation by these factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of evidence base (outcome frequency and sample populations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Meta-analytic conclusions are constrained by the available studies: some health outcomes are infrequently studied and most studies focus on healthy populations (students or community members).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify understudied outcomes (e.g., allergy symptom reductions, rate of disease progression) and advocate for more research with unhealthy and clinical samples as well as adolescents. Acknowledge that scarcity of studies limits confidence in conclusions for these areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental paradigm standards (measurement timing, manipulation checks, within- vs between-subjects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical experimental paradigms measure well-being and physiological variables at baseline, manipulate mood/emotion, assess physiological variables post-manipulation, and include manipulation checks; designs include within-subjects (repeated measures) or between-subjects with random assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow rigorous procedures: measure baselines, perform manipulation checks immediately after inductions, use appropriate analytic methods (repeated measures ANOVA, change scores, control for baseline). Consider sample size and counterbalancing (examples: pictures used to induce mood; blood draws at baseline and post-manipulation; continuous monitoring of heart rate and blood pressure). Use multilevel modeling for within- and between-person changes when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-regression interpretation and application
rubrics_metrics.description: Meta-regression coefficients (intercept b0 and slope b1) should be written out as regression equations to predict effect sizes from moderators (e.g., proportion male).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the regression equation y = b0 + b1(X) where X is the moderator (e.g., proportion male from 0.00 to 1.00). Apply coefficients to predict effect sizes for samples with different characteristics (example provided: predicted effect size for immune functioning decreases as sample becomes more male). Present and interpret meta-regression results concretely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical and public-health interpretation of effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate statistical effect sizes into practical public-health implications (e.g., increased survival probabilities, changes in mortality risk, implications for healthcare utilization and costs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating benefits of well-being interventions, weigh costs of improving well-being against benefits such as lives saved and reduced morbidity. Frame effects in terms meaningful to policy and clinical decision-makers (probability changes, OR/RR, potential impacts on healthcare costs).
